text_blocks.snippet: Ophthalmic migraine, also known as ocular migraine, is characterized by visual disturbances that can include shimmering or flashing lights, zigzag lines, blind spots, or temporary vision loss. These visual symptoms may or may not be accompanied by a headache. Other possible symptoms include nausea, vomiting, and dizziness.
snippet_highlighted_words: visual disturbances that can include shimmering or flashing lights, zigzag lines, blind spots, or temporary vision loss

list.title: Flashes or Flickers of Light:
list.snippet: These can appear as brief, shimmering, or flashing sensations in the field of vision.

list.title: Zigzag Lines:
list.snippet: These can appear as bright, jagged, or shimmering lines, often described as a "heat haze" effect.

list.title: Blind Spots or Scotomas:
list.snippet: These are areas of vision loss that can be small and expand over time or be stationary.

list.title: Temporary Vision Loss:
list.snippet: In some cases, a person may experience temporary blindness in one or both eyes.

list.title: Blurred Vision:
list.snippet: This can be a symptom of an ocular migraine, making it difficult to focus or see clearly.

list.title: Headache:
list.snippet: While not all ophthalmic migraines are accompanied by a headache, some individuals may experience a headache, which can be throbbing or pulsating.

list.title: Nausea and Vomiting:
list.snippet: These are common symptoms that can occur during or after the visual disturbances.

list.title: Dizziness or Lightheadedness:
list.snippet: Some people may feel dizzy or lightheaded during an ocular migraine episode.

list.title: Eye Pain:
list.snippet: In some instances, individuals may experience pain or tenderness around the affected eye.
If visual symptoms are severe or persist for more than an hour.
If new visual symptoms develop, especially if accompanied by other symptoms like speech difficulties or weakness on one side of the body.
If visual symptoms are accompanied by a severe headache, especially if it's a sudden, intense headache.
If visual symptoms are accompanied by other symptoms like facial drooping, arm weakness, or slurred speech (which could indicate a stroke).
If you've never experienced ocular migraine symptoms before.
If the symptoms interfere with daily activities.

text_blocks.snippet: It's important to note that ocular migraines are usually benign and resolve on their own, but it's crucial to rule out more serious conditions that may mimic the symptoms.
